leads.text: Attacker-controlled OBJECT PROPERTY NAMES are never sanitized. In lib/sanitize.js:42 the object branch does `Object.keys(data).forEach((key) => { ... data[key] = sanitizeHtml(item, ...) ... })` -- only the VALUE at each key is passed through sanitizeHtml; the key string itself is never rewritten or validated. Attacker input reaches here from index.js:9 (`req[k] = sanitize(req[k], options)` for body/params/headers) and index.js:12 (`sanitize(req.query, options)`). So a request body/query of the form {"": "benign"} passes completely through the middleware with the HTML payload intact in the key. Any consuming app that renders or echoes request-object keys (e.g. iterating req.body to build an HTML form/table, or serializing the object into a template) gets stored/reflected XSS despite the sanitizer being installed. This defeats the library's stated contract that everything in req is XSS-safe.

No call site anywhere takes `key` as an argument. Full body from CpgCall uid bfeb99f0a876d656062b037399e27cee15711f57 (lib/sanitize.js:42, reachable_from_entry=true, hop=1): "Object.keys(data).forEach((key) => { if (options.allowedKeys.includes(key)) { return; } const item = data[key]; if (typeof item === 'string') { data[key] = sanitizeHtml(item, options.sanitizerOptions); } else if (Array.isArray(item) || typeof item === 'object') { data[key] = sanitize(options, item); } })". leads.text: The hardened own-property guard `hasOwn(object, key)` (lib/sanitize.js:5-8), built deliberately with `Reflect.ownKeys(object).filter(item => typeof item !== 'symbol')` + `keys.includes(key)` specifically so inherited/prototype-chain keys cannot satisfy it, is applied ONLY to the trusted developer-supplied `options` object inside `initializeOptions` (lines 12, 16, 21 — exactly 3 callsites, no others in the graph). It is never applied in `sanitize()` (lines 41-53), which is the function that walks the ATTACKER-controlled request data. There, keys come from raw `Object.keys(data)` (line 42) and are written straight back with a computed member assignment `data[key] = ...` (lines 48 and 50) with zero `__proto__`/`constructor`/`prototype` filtering anywhere in the repo. The anti-prototype-chain protection sits 35 lines above the live vulnerable write and is pointed at the one input that is NOT untrusted. Result: prototype pollution via the sanitizer itself.

Failure scenario: body-parser/express.json() parses with JSON.parse, which creates a genuine OWN property named "__proto__". Object.keys() enumerates it, so `data["__proto__"] = sanitize(options, item)` invokes the Object.prototype.__proto__ SETTER instead of writing an own property, re-pointing data's prototype at the attacker's object. POST {"__proto__":{"isAdmin":"x"}} therefore yields req.body.isAdmin === "x" while Object.keys(req.body) stays empty — a silent auth/logic-bypass primitive handed to downstream code that believes the object was sanitized. Applies to req.body, req.params, req.headers (index.js:7-9) and req.query (index.js:12).

leads.text: Unbounded attacker-controlled recursion depth -> stack-exhaustion DoS. The `sanitize` function recurses at lib/sanitize.js:36 (`sanitize(options, item)` inside the Array.map branch) and lib/sanitize.js:50 (`sanitize(options, item)` inside the object branch) with NO depth counter, NO visited-set, and NO cycle guard -- the function's only parameters are `options` and `data`. Attacker fully controls nesting depth of a JSON body (body-parser is a declared dependency) or of a bracketed query string, so a request like {"a":{"a":{"a": ... }}} nested a few thousand levels deep drives recursion past the V8 stack limit, throwing a RangeError inside the synchronous middleware before next() at index.js:19 -- an unhandled exception per request, giving cheap remote DoS of every route behind the middleware.

leads.text: `allowedKeys` is a DEEP skip, not a shallow one, silently exempting whole attacker-controlled subtrees. At lib/sanitize.js:43-45 the object branch does `if (options.allowedKeys.includes(key)) { return; }` -- the bare `return` exits the forEach callback BEFORE `const item = data[key]` and before any sanitizeHtml/recursion, so when a key is allow-listed the entire nested object/array underneath it is left completely unsanitized, not merely that key's own scalar value. A developer who allow-lists a container field (e.g. allowedKeys:['content'] or ['meta']) to permit one rich-text value unknowingly disables sanitization for every descendant value of that subtree, so attacker HTML at req.body.meta.anything.deep reaches the app raw. Compounding this, the check is applied at EVERY recursion level (the same `options.allowedKeys` is consulted for nested objects), so an allow-listed name occurring anywhere in the tree exempts that subtree too.

leads.text: Incomplete source coverage: `req.cookies` is never sanitized. index.js:7 iterates the hardcoded list `['body','params','headers']` and index.js:12 handles `req.query` separately -- that is the complete set of request surfaces touched by the middleware. `req.cookies` / `req.signedCookies` (cookie-parser), and `req.url`/`req.originalUrl`/`req.path`, are attacker-controlled inputs that pass through the middleware entirely untouched. An application that trusts the middleware's blanket 'req is sanitized' guarantee and renders a cookie value gets XSS. Additionally, the truthiness guard `if (req[k])` at index.js:8 makes the body case fail SILENTLY (no error, no warning) when the middleware is mounted before body-parser, since req.body is then undefined and the key is skipped.

leads.text: `req.params` sanitization is likely a no-op under the declared Express 5 dependency when the middleware is mounted globally. index.js:9 writes the sanitized copy back with `req[k] = sanitize(req[k], options)` for k='params', but with express ^5.0.1 the router populates/overwrites `req.params` per matched route AFTER global `app.use` middleware has already run, so the sanitized object is discarded and route handlers observe raw, unsanitized `req.params` values. Note the author clearly knew about this class of problem for query -- index.js:13 deliberately uses `Object.defineProperty(req, 'query', {writable:false, configurable:true, ...})` to pin the sanitized query against Express 5's getter -- yet applied no equivalent protection to params, which is the surface the router rewrites latest. Ranked lower because confirming the overwrite ordering requires reading Express 5 router internals, which are outside this scan.

leads.text: Fail-open on the strictest configuration: initializeOptions() only forwards allowedTags into sanitizerOptions when `options.allowedTags.length > 0`, and only forwards allowedAttributes when `Object.keys(options.allowedAttributes).length > 0`. A developer who explicitly requests the MOST restrictive policy -- `allowedTags: []` (strip every tag) or `allowedAttributes: {}` (strip every attribute) -- has that setting silently discarded, leaving sanitizerOptions without the key, so sanitize-html falls back to its built-in permissive default allowlist instead of stripping everything. The requested control is silently disabled rather than enforced; the app believes all HTML is removed while a default tag/attribute allowlist is actually in force.

Line 12 guards allowedTags with `Array.isArray(options.allowedTags)` before use, but line 16 calls `Object.keys(options.allowedAttributes)` with only a hasOwn() presence check and no type guard. If allowedAttributes is present but null (or a primitive), Object.keys(null) throws a TypeError at middleware-construction/first-use time. leads.text: index.js:13-18 installs the sanitized query with `Object.defineProperty(req, 'query', { value: sanitizedQuery, writable: false, configurable: true, enumerable: true })`. The `writable: false` is unambiguous protective intent — lock the sanitized query so later code cannot swap it back to raw input — but `configurable: true` on the very same descriptor completely reverts that protection: a configurable property can be redefined by any later middleware or route handler via another Object.defineProperty, or deleted and re-assigned. The lock is explicitly shipped unlocked, one line below the line that sets it. This is a protection that is present, visible, and neutered in place.

leads.text: The `xss` Express middleware in index.js decides which parts of the request to sanitize from a hardcoded literal worklist `['body', 'params', 'headers']` (line 7), plus a separate explicit pass over `req.query` (line 12). The literal omits `cookies`. The result is an incomplete disallowed-input list: an application that mounts this middleware as `app.use(xss())` — the package's advertised purpose — gets body/params/headers/query sanitized but `req.cookies` passed through completely unsanitized, while the middleware's name implies full-request XSS protection. Attacker-controlled cookie values (settable via a reflected Set-Cookie, a sibling-subdomain write, or any prior XSS) therefore reach downstream render/send sinks with HTML intact. I confirmed the string 'cookie' occurs zero times anywhere in the scanned repo, so no other code path compensates. Exploitability in a given deployment requires the host app to populate req.cookies (e.g. cookie-parser, which is NOT among the declared Dependency nodes) and to render a cookie value, which is why this is MEDIUM rather than HIGH.

leads.text: Components-with-known-vulnerabilities / dependency-hygiene lead, derived purely from the declared Dependency nodes. Two concerns: (1) `sanitize-html` is tilde-pinned at `~2.13.0`, which resolves only to >=2.13.0 <2.14.0 — this is the single security-critical component in the package (it performs all actual HTML sanitization at lib/sanitize.js:28/33/48), and the tilde pin structurally blocks uptake of any fix shipped in 2.14.x or later. (2) `body-parser` is declared at `^1.19.0`, a floor that predates the hardening done across the 1.20.x line (including the urlencoded-extended resource-exhaustion fix), and it is a redundant direct dependency given `express` is declared at `^5.0.1` and ships its own body parsing — so the app may run a second, older parser than the one Express vendors. I am reporting the exact declared version strings I queried and flagging them for cross-check against an advisory database; I am deliberately NOT asserting a specific CVE identifier as fact, since I cannot query advisory data from this graph. A verifier should resolve the installed lockfile versions and diff them against GHSA/NVD for sanitize-html 2.13.x, body-parser 1.19.x-1.20.x, and express 5.0.1.
